newsitem.title: HUNGARY: TRACTEBEL HUNGARY TALKS NEED MORE TIME - OFFICIALS.
newsitem.headline: TRACTEBEL HUNGARY TALKS NEED MORE TIME - OFFICIALS.

text.p: Talks between Belgian utility Tractebel and the Hungarian government over the future of Tractebel's Hungarian investments are expected to continue for at least another week, officials said on Wednesday.
"A number of questions are still to be resolved and both sides are to meet again later this week," Hungarian state privatisation agency (APV) spokesman Adam Dudits told Reuters.

Tractebel, which bought 48 percent of the oil-fired Dunamenti power station in December 1995, is negotiating with APV over the price it is to receive for the power the plant supplies to the Hungary's electricity company MVM, which sells on the electricity to the regional distributors.
Both sides had said originally they expected negotiations to be completed by the end of January.

The Belgian company claims it is making huge losses on the Dunamenti operation as it buys its oil from Hungarian oil company MOL at market rates but sells electricity to MVM at a fixed price set by the government.

It says the 34.5 percent increase it was granted for its energy last month will not even cover its costs and has threatened to seek legal action to recover its $141 million investment if it cannot secure an eight percent profit margin stipulated in the privatisation contract.
However, late in January, APV chairman Arpad Kovacs said APV had submitted a written proposal to Tractebel which is believed to have formed the basis for further discussions.
Dudits confirmed that the document was being discussed but could not reveal any further details.

Tibor Kuhl, Tractebel's representative in Hungary, confirmed to Reuters that talks would continue. "We can tell you something in a couple of a weeks -- these things sometimes take longer than you expect."

Other Western investors such as Electricite de France (EdF), Gaz de France and German electricity giant RWE have bought large stakes in the energy distribution sector and were also promised an eight percent return on investment.

They have appealed to the government over January energy price rises for consumers of 24.9 percent for electricity and 18.8 percent for gas which they say are insufficient to assure the profit margin.
However, only Tractebel has raised the spectre of legal action to recoup its entire investment.
A report by the Hungarian State Audit Office published on Monday criticised the government for failing to properly evaluate Dunamenti's assets prior to the its sale to Tractebel.
It also described APV's insistence on a cash sale as "contradictory to current professional and government principles".
